ety.text: From Middle English noen, none, non, from Old English nōn (“the ninth hour”), from a Germanic borrowing of classical Latin nōna (“ninth hour”) (short for nōna hōra), feminine of nōnus (“ninth”). Cognate with Dutch noen, obsolete German Non, Norwegian non.

senses.d: The time of day when the Sun seems to reach its highest point in the sky; solar noon.
ex: On Saturdays, I love to have a lie-in until noon.
The race is due to start at noon sharp.

senses.d: The mean time of solar noon, marked as twelve o'clock on most clocks.
The corresponding time in the middle of the night; midnight.
ex: So the sad mother at the noon of night / From bloody Memphis stole her silent flight […].
When night was at its noon I heard a voice chanting the Koran in sweetest accents […].

senses.d: The ninth hour of the day counted from sunrise; around three o'clock in the afternoon.

ex: In the very noon of that brilliant life which was destined to be so soon, and so fatally, overshadowed.

senses.d: To relax or sleep around midday.
The letter ن in the Arabic script.

fr:midi.gl: noon, midday (time of the day at which the sun reaches its highest point)

ety.text: Inherited from Old French midi, from mi (“middle”) + di (“day”).
From mezzo- + giorno. Compare Catalan migjorn, Romanian miazăzi.

Latin mediusslbor. Old Spanish medio Spanish medio Spanish día Spanish mediodía From medio (“half”) + día (“day”). Compare Occitan mieidia, French midi, Portuguese meio-dia, Catalan migdia, Italian mezzodì, Romanian miazăzi.
